overview: Two opposite steps of urine formation in the kidney — one pushes fluid out of the blood, the other pulls useful substances back in.
genZNote: Filtration: dumping everything out of the blood first. Reabsorption: quickly grabbing back everything the body still needs.

aspects.label: Location
aspects.valueA: Occurs in the glomerulus, within Bowman's capsule.
aspects.valueB: Occurs mainly along the proximal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle, and distal tubule.

aspects.label: Direction of Movement
aspects.valueA: Blood plasma components move from glomerular capillaries into the nephron.
aspects.valueB: Useful substances move from the filtrate in the tubule back into the blood.

aspects.label: Selectivity
aspects.valueA: Relatively non-selective — filters based on molecular size (small molecules pass, large proteins/cells don't).
aspects.valueB: Highly selective — actively reclaims glucose, amino acids, most water, and ions.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: Normally, glucose is 100% reabsorbed — glucose in urine (glycosuria) signals the reabsorption capacity has been exceeded, as in diabetes.
overlay.memoryTrick: Filtration throws stuff out first. Reabsorption takes the good stuff back.
overlay.commonMisconception: Filtration at the glomerulus is not selective for what the body needs — it's a size-based sieve, so useful molecules like glucose are filtered out too and must be reabsorbed.
